content.rendered:
On Monday, Sept. 14, the U.S. Supreme Court issued an unsigned order preserving a lower-court ruling that barred the United States Postal Service (USPS) from enacting new mail-in-voting regulations.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in late March calling for the USPS to use state-specific lists of residents who are U.S. citizens to regulate mail ballots. This involved changes to their website. As of Sept. 3, the USPS was still “making updates to the portal,” according to CBS News. 

“There’s a power struggle about who sets the rules for elections, and the president was attempting to use his power over the Postal Service, which is the power the president has, to effectively make rules for elections, which is a power that the courts have found lies with Congress and especially with states,” said William McGeveran, the dean of the University of Minnesota’s Law School.

Massachusetts-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani blocked the USPS from moving forward with some aspects of the order, but the Supreme Court ruled that Talwani’s decision was premature. In an unsigned 6-3 ruling on Aug. 24, the high court said no decisions could be made because the USPS had not yet moved forward with its plans. 

Talwani continued to fight back by issuing a preliminary injunction on August 27, which blocked the Trump administration from requiring states to comply with the rules as the legal challenges continued, according to CBS News. 

“USPS leadership, it appears, has discarded all best practices as they speed the project to be ready for a September 1 implementation — raising questions about whether catastrophic failure would be a feature rather than a bug,” said a disclosure put out on Aug. 31 by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit organization representing the anonymous USPS employee with detailed knowledge of the new system. 

 The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to intervene in the case, and on September 14 the court put out an unsigned order stating, “The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction. And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this Court do not favor a stay.” 

The Supreme Court issued an unsigned order because it was not making an official ruling on whether the changes to voting procedure are constitutional. Instead, it allowed Talwani to continue her challenge of Trump’s order.

“What the Supreme Court really did was refuse to get involved, and let the lower court’s rulings stand. Which is important because it means it doesn’t necessarily indicate for certain how the court would rule if this ever came back to them on the merits,” said McGeveran.

 “I was surprised because I feel like this Supreme Court has set a precedent of siding with a lot of far right policies,” said Asha Huzurbazar ’28. The decision followed existing precedent on dissolving lower court injunctions. It considered whether the Judge, in this case, Talwani, could prove the order would cause irreparable harm if implemented, and whether the order would be unconstitutional if it went to court after implementation.

“Today, the Supreme Court protected one of our most fundamental, inalienable rights — the right to make your voice heard at the ballot box,” said Attorney General Letitia James, one of the Democratic officials who sued over the mail-voting rules. “This last-minute change could have thrown our elections into chaos, and I am truly relieved the Court granted this reprieve.”

“It’s quite overwhelming, and it’s a very convoluted situation. So the headline is: nothing has actually changed,” said the head of CarlsVote, Lizzie Appelbaum ’28.
